description: Divergence Atlas is a two-person team combining mathematical physics, machine learning and software engineering.
summary:
Is that a lasting climate trend, or just a few unusually hot, wet or dry years? Divergence Atlas helps anyone find out.

Headlines say the climate is changing, but every year differs from the last, and a few unusual years can look like a trend. Divergence Atlas is a free web tool that tests whether a change in Earth system data is real, and explains the answer in plain English.

You pick one of 12 questions (for example, precipitation, heat, cloud cover or soil wetness), then choose a place on the map, an area around it, or compare two places. The tool fetches live NASA POWER monthly data, removes the seasonal cycle, and tests for a long-term trend. It reports the change per decade with a 95% confidence interval and a p-value corrected for month-to-month persistence, which otherwise causes false alarms. It also estimates how many years of data would be needed to confirm the trend.

Sometimes the honest answer is "no clear trend", and the tool says so. It also states its limits: values are grid cells, not stations, and a trend does not prove a cause.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Divergence Atlas helps you find out whether a change in Earth system data is real. You choose one of 12 questions: precipitation, soil wetness, relative and specific humidity, mean temperature, daytime highs, night-time lows, surface temperature, sunlight, cloud cover, wind or surface pressure. Then you pick a place on the map, an area around it (about 100 to 1,000 km), or two places to compare. You can also filter by season or upload your own NASA CSV file.

HOW IT WORKS

The server fetches live monthly data from the NASA POWER API. In the browser, each month is compared with the usual value for that calendar month, which removes the seasonal cycle and leaves only the change. The trend is estimated with the Theil-Sen slope and a 95% confidence interval. Significance is tested with Mann-Kendall, adjusted for month-to-month persistence, which otherwise causes false alarms. The tool also estimates how many years of data would be needed to confirm the trend (Weatherhead et al., 1998). You get a plain-English headline, a chart showing the trend and its 95% range, a verdict, and an Explain panel that also lists what the result does not tell you.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Anyone can check a climate claim for their own place in minutes, with no code and no account. It is built for students, teachers, journalists and curious citizens who want a straight answer.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- It starts from a question, not from a dataset or a file.

- It gives an honest verdict, including "no clear trend", instead of only drawing a line.

- It tells you how long a record you would need to be sure.

- It compares two places and says whether they diverge.

VALIDITY

Slope and test statistics match SciPy and pymannkendall. In simulation (300 series per case, 30 years of monthly data), the adjusted test gave about 4% false alarms, against 22-52% without the adjustment.

TOOLS

Python (Flask, gunicorn, requests), hosted on Render, with the code on GitHub. JavaScript, HTML and CSS in the browser, with Chart.js for charts and Leaflet for maps. Place search uses OpenStreetMap Nominatim, and map tiles come from Esri. All data comes from NASA POWER.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

- The interface is in English, needs no login, and uses a blue and orange palette that works for colour-blind users.

- Units are shown on every card and chart.

- Limits are stated openly: values are grid cells rather than stations, area results are an average of 9 grid points, soil wetness is a model estimate, trends are linear only, and a trend does not prove a cause.

AI ASSISTANCE

Code and text were written with assistance from Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by the author.
